content: Tropomyosin alpha-1 chain is a protein encoded by the TPM1 gene in humans. This gene belongs to the tropomyosin (Tm) family, which consists of highly conserved and widely distributed actin-binding proteins. These proteins play a critical role in the contractile systems of both striated and smooth muscles, as well as in the cytoskeletal structure of non-muscle cells. Tropomyosin (Tm) is a protein with a molecular weight of 32.7 kDa and is composed of 284 amino acids. It exists as a flexible homodimer or heterodimer, consisting of two alpha-helical chains. These chains adopt a bent coiled-coil conformation, allowing them to wrap around seven actin molecules within a functional unit of muscle. Tm polymerizes end-to-end along the two grooves of actin filaments, providing structural stability to the filaments. In human striated muscles, Tm is expressed from three genes: TPM1 (α-Tm), TPM2 (β-Tm), and TPM3 (γ-Tm). Among these, α-Tm is the predominant isoform in striated muscle. In human cardiac muscle, the ratio of α-Tm to β-Tm is approximately 5:1. Tropomyosin plays a regulatory role in muscle contraction by working in conjunction with the troponin complex. It modulates the calcium-dependent interaction between actin and myosin. Tm molecules are arranged in a head-to-tail configuration along the actin thin filament and are essential for the cooperative activation of muscle contraction. A three-state model, proposed by McKillop and Geeves, describes the positional changes of Tm during the cardiac cycle. In the blocked (B) state, which occurs during diastole when intracellular calcium levels are low, Tm obstructs the myosin-binding site on actin. In the closed (C) state, Tm is positioned on the inner groove of actin, allowing myosin to adopt a cocked position where its heads are weakly bound to actin and not generating force. In the myosin-binding (M) state, Tm is further displaced from actin by strongly bound myosin crossbridges, which actively generate force. In addition to actin, Tm also binds to troponin T (TnT), which anchors the overlapping regions of adjacent Tm molecules to actin. Mutations in the TPM1 gene have been implicated in the development of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and dilated cardiomyopathy. In cases of HCM, mutations are often concentrated around the N-terminal region and a key actin-binding region known as period 5.
